t:
(a) 
The Attorney General shall, within six months of date of enactment of this Act, issue guidelines for the procedures to be employed by any Federal officer or employee, in connection with the investigation or prosecution of an offense, to obtain documentary materials in the private possession of a person when the person is not reasonably believed to be a suspect in such offense or related by blood or marriage to such a suspect, and when the materials sought are not contraband or the fruits or instrumentalities of an offense. The Attorney General shall incorporate in such guidelines—

        (1) 
a recognition of the personal privacy interests of the person in possession of such documentary materials;
 
        (2) 
a requirement that the least intrusive method or means of obtaining such materials be used which do not substantially jeopardize the availability or usefulness of the materials sought to be obtained;
 
        (3) 
a recognition of special concern for privacy interests in cases in which a search or seizure for such documents would intrude upon a known confidential relationship such as that which may exist between clergyman and parishioner; lawyer and client; or doctor and patient; and
 
        (4) 
a requirement that an application for a warrant to conduct a search governed by this title be approved by an attorney for the government, except that in an emergency situation the application may be approved by another appropriate supervisory official if within 24 hours of such emergency the appropriate United States Attorney is notified.
  
    (b) The Attorney General shall collect and compile information on, and report annually to the Committees on the Judiciary of the Senate and the House of Representatives on the use of search warrants by Federal officers and employees for documentary materials described in subsection (a)(3).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that issuing guidelines amounts to rulemaking, or that the annual report is a participatory process. But the guidelines are internal procedures directing federal officers and employees, with no comment period, hearing, or consultation with any outside party, and the report goes to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. The call is uncertain only because guidelines could be treated as akin to regulations.
fable.s: The Attorney General shall, within six months of date of enactment of this Act, issue guidelines for the procedures to be employed by any Federal officer or employee

qwen_block.w: This section requires the Attorney General to issue internal guidelines for federal officers and to report to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. The guidelines themselves are internal procedural rules for federal employees and do not require consultation with or input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before the decision is made.
qwen_block.s: The Attorney General shall collect and compile information on, and report annually to the Committees on the Judiciary of the Senate and the House of Representatives on the use of search warrants by Federal officers and employees for documentary materials described in subsection (a)(3).

opus.w: Every actor in this section is federal. The Attorney General writes internal guidelines for federal officers, government attorneys approve warrant applications, and reports go to congressional committees. The tempting reading treats the guidelines as rulemaking that brings in outsiders, but this section requires no public comment, hearing, or consultation with anyone outside the government. Private people's privacy interests are only something the guidelines must recognize, not a role in the decision.
opus.s: The Attorney General shall collect and compile information on, and report annually to the Committees on the Judiciary of the Senate and the House of Representatives on the use of search warrants by Federal officers and employees
opus.b: 1. **Reasoning.** The tempting reading is that "issue guidelines" counts as rulemaking, which would make this "Yes." That reading fails because these guidelines govern how federal officers and employees obtain documentary materials. They are internal procedures for federal staff, and nothing in this section requires notice-and-comment or any outside input. The other procedural pieces stay inside the federal government too. Warrant applications are approved by a government attorney or supervisor, with notice to the U.S. Attorney. The annual report goes to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees, which are part of Congress. The "personal privacy interests" of private people are things the guidelines must take into account, not a way for those people to take part in the decision. One caveat: the related next section of the code (42 U.S.C. 2000aa-12) does subject these guidelines to the public rulemaking procedure in 5 U.S.C. 553. That text is not in this section, so I have lowered my confidence.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires the Attorney General to issue internal guidelines for federal officers and to report to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, and the guidelines are for internal use by federal employees. There is no requirement to consult with or coordinate with any outside parties (such as the public, states, or private individuals) before making a decision. The mention of privacy interests is a factor for federal officers to consider, not a mechanism for outside participation.
qwen_chat.s: The Attorney General shall, within six months of date of enactment of this Act, issue guidelines for the procedures to be employed by any Federal officer or employee... The Attorney General shall collect and compile information on, and report annually to the Committees on the Judiciary of the Senate and the House of Representatives...
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement to recognize "personal privacy interests" or "confidential relationships" implies a process where the affected individuals (clergy, lawyers, patients) participate in the decision-making. However, the text only requires the Attorney General to issue internal guidelines for federal officers; it does not mandate that the individuals whose privacy is at stake be consulted or given a voice in the specific decision to search. The "participation" is not with the outsiders, but rather a directive to federal employees to consider certain factors.

Another tempting reading is that the report to Congress constitutes participation. However, Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to them is not participation as defined.

The section describes internal procedural guidelines for federal law enforcement and reporting requirements to Congress. It does not require consultation with, or input from, any party outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private individuals) before a decision is made. The "person in possession" is the subject of the search, not a participant in the decision to search.
